transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: The Hive Blight [H-02], Order of the Dry Saint [F-02].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the reed roofs of Hollowmoot's outskirts as you haul a borrowed skiff up to the Ashwater tollgate, its chains dripping rust-red into the flood. Torches gutter behind a slumped barricade of sandbags and old doors; two Warden sentries huddle under an oilcloth, crossbows more for show than confidence at this hour. Somewhere behind you in the punt, a stranger you pulled from the water an hour ago mutters in his sleep — a low, wordless tune that makes the hair on your arms rise. The Wardens haven't heard it yet. You have maybe a hundred yards of black water and torchlight between you and finding out what they'll do when they do.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Ho there! Bit of a night to be standing watch—the flood's climbing something fierce. Any word when they'll open the Causeway again?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra guides the skiff toward the torchlight with practiced ease, sitting tall in the bow. She raises a hand in greeting to the sentries, her voice bright and easy as the rain drums down. She's calling to them like she knows them—because she does. Act natural. Get closer. Keep them talking.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Easy now, friend. We're going to be fine—just keep quiet for me, yes?

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock poles the skiff forward with steady urgency, leaning down to grip the stranger's shoulder and ground him. Her jaw is tight as she locks eyes on the Wardens' torchlight ahead. She's done business with these men before, and none of it was good. But she won't show them fear or hesitation. Whatever this man is, whoever pulled him from the water, he's in her care now. She moves the skiff forward like she owns this black water, like she's done this hundred times before.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Ashwater gate. Need high ground before the weather turns worse. Pulled this one from the water maybe an hour back.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow poles the skiff with practiced ease toward the torchlight, his movements deliberate and open. Behind him, Brack shifts uneasily at the bow, ears flat, a low growl rumbling under the rain. The stranger's muttering has quieted to almost nothing, but something about them still sets the hound's hackles on end. Yarrow keeps one hand on Brack's scruff, steadying them both while reading the water ahead and the two slumped sentries in their oilcloth. He knew these men once, before the disgrace, and he still carries that same bearing—the kind that says *I know what I'm doing here*.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Warden Sergeant Coy steps out from under the oilcloth at the sound of Yarrow's voice, squinting through the rain before recognition — old, complicated recognition — crosses his face. "Yarrow Weir-keeper... didn't figure to see you polling up out of the dark again." He waves the other sentry to lower his crossbow, but his eyes drift past you to the huddled shape in the skiff's bottom, and to Brack, whose growl hasn't let up. Petra's easy chatter about the toll and Caddock's steady hand on the stranger's shoulder buy you the yards you need — the skiff bumps up against the gate pilings, torchlight finally close enough to see faces clearly. Coy's gaze lingers a beat too long on the muttering man. "He sick?" he asks, flat, one hand drifting toward the chain-latch instead of away from it.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Just pulled him from the water, Coy—he's half-drowned and tired, nothing more. You know how the storm gets everyone wound up tonight.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra leans forward with practiced ease, the manner of someone who grew up at this gate. Her hand drifts toward her passage token, a casual gesture of familiarity and trust that speaks volumes to Coy.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: He's been in that cold water too long, that's all. Needs warmth, needs dry. I know what drowning does to people, Sergeant—I've pulled them back from it before. Let us through and he'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock keeps her hand firm on the stranger's shoulder, her body between him and Coy, meeting the Warden's gaze without flinching. Her voice carries the weight of a woman who's delivered children in worse conditions than this and won't be questioned about it. She doesn't move the skiff back; she waits, steady as stone.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Found him in the dark water, Sergeant, singing like nothing I've heard before. Brack won't settle, and Brack knows the difference between drowning men and something worse. I don't know what he is, but he needs shelter and light.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow meets Coy's gaze steadily, one hand still on Brack's scruff. He keeps his shoulders open, unthreatening, but doesn't look away from the Warden Sergeant—the kind of straight dealing that's kept his word good even through disgrace. He lets Coy see the tension in Brack, the hound's refusal to settle, because that's honest. Whatever this stranger is, Yarrow isn't going to pretend otherwise.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — create advantage with Rapport: dice + - - -, invoking Hears the swarm-song before others do [PE-03] → Good (+3) vs Good (+3): TIE

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: This man needs help, Coy—let us pass. Petra straightens, jaw set, meeting the Warden's gaze directly.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra refuses the compel on 'A Fisher's Stilt Hut'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's gesture toward her old passage token nearly works — Coy's eyes soften half a second at the familiar motion, the practiced ease of a girl who grew up at this very gate. But the tie doesn't tip clean her way: as her hand drifts to the token, the stranger in the skiff's bottom stirs and the wordless tune rises just loud enough to carry over the rain, the swarm-song unmistakable now that everyone's listening for it. Coy's fingers, already on the chain-latch, go white-knuckled around it instead of falling away. Petra sets her jaw and pushes forward anyway rather than let the moment cost her the stilt hut she keeps dry above the flood — she pays for that refusal in coin the Wardens understand: Coy's grip doesn't loosen, and he takes one wary step back toward the barricade, calling low over his shoulder for the other sentry to bring a torch closer, "for a proper look." The gate hasn't shut. But it hasn't opened either, and now four sets of eyes — Coy's, the second sentry's, and whatever's listening in that black water — are fixed on the sleeping man's face.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Wake up! Come on, stop singing!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra doesn't hesitate—she's heard the swarm-song before, and she knows exactly what it means. She lunges forward, grabs the stranger's shoulder, and shakes him hard, trying to snap him out of the song's grip before Coy locks them out.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm leans forward slightly in the stern, his eyes fixed on the stranger's face in the torchlight. He watches the rhythm of the humming, his jaw tightening slightly. His hand finds the blessed herbs and iron at his belt—a familiar weight. He remains silent, waiting.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: The swamp water scrambles people's minds, Sergeant. I've brought a hundred back from worse. Let us through and he'll be fine by sunrise.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock's hand stays firm on the stranger's shoulder. She meets Coy's eyes without flinching—the steady gaze of someone who knows what she's looking at, who's handled this a hundred times before. She doesn't move the skiff back. Doesn't soften. She simply holds her ground, letting her bearing do what words alone cannot: *I know what I'm doing here.*)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: That's the swarm-song, Sergeant—he's touched. We get him inside where there's light and fire, or the blight spreads. Your gate's the wall now. Open it.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow keeps one hand steady on Brack's scruff, the other gripping his pole. He doesn't advance the skiff but doesn't retreat, meeting Coy's eyes with the kind of quiet certainty that comes from someone who knows this threat better than most. His voice is low and final—not urgent, but clear as an order from a man still accustomed to being heard when it matters. Brack's growl subsides to a low rumble, but the hound's ears stay flat, his body tense against Yarrow's leg. The message is unmistakable: Yarrow understands what's at stake, and if he's asking Coy to open that gate, there's a reason the old Warden should listen.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Athletics: dice 0 + 0 + → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's hand cracks across the stranger's cheek and he jerks upright with a gasp, the wordless tune dying in his throat mid-note like a snapped harp string. For one long breath the only sound is rain on oilcloth — then the man blinks, coughs up swamp water, and asks in a cracked, ordinary voice where he is. Whatever had its hook in him, it's let go, at least for now. Sergeant Coy's white knuckles finally loosen on the chain-latch; he lets out a breath he'd clearly been holding since the singing started, and mutters something about "just a fever-touched fool, not the sickness proper," more to convince himself than anyone else. He waves the second sentry's torch back and hauls the gate chain up hand over hand, the old iron groaning as it rises. "Get him dry, Yarrow, and get gone before I think better of this," Coy says, not quite meeting anyone's eyes — old loyalty winning out over duty, this once. The skiff slides through under the dripping chains, Hollowmoot's lantern-glow finally within reach, the stranger shivering and bewildered but alive, and very much still yours to answer for.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: My cousin Edren—he was learning the weir-craft with me before the flood took him. Before the waters rose too high, he asked me if we'd find out together what had gone wrong with the old channels. I promised him we would. Now he's here in the Death-House, and I read his name aloud every time I come, honoring that oath to him and to all the others who can't speak for themselves anymore.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I'm not moving this pole until every name that drowned here has been read aloud—not for the Wardens, not for anyone. Edren deserves to be remembered by more than silence and rain.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts the compel on 'Duty to the Dead'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: Shelter at Yarrow offers the Death-House on Hollowmoot's north stilts — a cramped, dry chapel-hut where he still guards the drowned bodies of the parish, refusing to let the flood take them unnamed. Rows of shrouded dead line the walls, and he insists they won't mind sharing their roof with the living for one night. hides What the Death-House actually hides is that it's already on the Wardens' burn-list — quietly marked days ago after a hive-touched corpse was found among the dead Yarrow tends, and the torch crew was only ever waiting on the rain to break before putting it to flame..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The Death-House squats on its north stilts above the flood, low and close, rain drumming a steady percussion on cedar shingles that have somehow stayed whole. Inside it's dry — blessedly, achingly dry — and Yarrow moves among the shrouded rows like a man in a church he built himself, murmuring names as he passes, hand brushing linen-wrapped shoulders. Edren's shroud sits nearest the door, and Yarrow says his name last, voice cracking only slightly. The dead don't smell of rot so much as brine and reed-must, and for a moment it's almost peaceful — until someone notices one shroud, near the back wall, tied differently than the rest, its ropes newer, its knots hurried. Outside, the rain has thinned to a drizzle, and somewhere down the causeway a bell that isn't Saint Orrin's begins, faintly, to toll — the kind of toll that means torches are being lit.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: That's not Saint Orrin's bell—the Wardens' torch-crew! This place is marked for burning tonight, Yarrow. How many more names can you read before the fire comes?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's entire stance shifts at the unfamiliar bell-toll. Her hand moves to her pass-token by reflex, then drops. Her eyes are bright with the terrible knowledge of a girl raised among warnings. She's calculating—time, danger, the shrouded rows. She doesn't move to flee yet; she waits to see what Yarrow will do.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That knot-work is fresh. And listen—that bell. They're coming.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm's head snaps up at the distant bell toll. He crosses to the back wall where the differently-tied shroud lies, his movements precise and practiced. He leans in to examine the knots—newer rope, hastily wound—and traces the wrapping with practiced fingers, reading the corpse like scripture.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: That's a Warden bell. They're coming to burn this place. And that shroud there—one of the touched. They won't have it while I'm here.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock's head snaps up at the faint bell tolling down the causeway—not a saint's bell, not a funeral toll, but the sharp high call that means Wardens are lighting torches. She's heard it before. She strides to the back wall and kneels beside the shroud with the hastily-tied ropes, her weathered hands tracing the knots. When she looks up at Yarrow, her jaw is set.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: That bell isn't for blessing the dead—it's the Wardens' mark for fire. And these knots... someone put this shroud here after the others, trying to hide what's underneath.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow strides back through the rows of shrouded dead to the rear wall, rain-damp and urgent. His weathered fingers trace the hasty knots—newer rope, tied in haste and fear, nothing like the careful reverence he laid across Edren. He works at the bindings, jaw tight. Outside, the tolling grows sharper. Torches bob at the base of the north stilts, and boots thud on the causeway planks, climbing fast.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I don't care if they're climbing the stilts right now—I won't leave this body to burn unnamed and forgotten. Not after they went to such trouble to hide it. Someone put this one here in secret, and that means *something*. That means it matters.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — create advantage with Investigate: dice - 0 - -, invoking Trained to purge the hive from flesh himself [AN-04] → Fair (+2) vs Fair (+2): TIE

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Holy ground. This body, this soul—they deserve blessing, not ash. I stand witness and guardian tonight, and no Warden torch crosses this threshold.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Burning Religious Zeal'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Anselm's fingers work the hasty knots loose even as his reading falters — the rope binds oddly, doubled back on itself like whoever tied it was shaking. The shroud falls open at the shoulder, and there's no mistaking what's underneath: grey-veined skin, a wound gone black and weeping, features slack in the particular stillness of the hive-touched dead. Caddock is already on her knees beside it, murmuring something that isn't quite a prayer, one hand raised as if daring anyone to move the body. Outside, the bell stops. Boots hit the base of the north stilts — many boots — and torchlight flares orange through the seams in the shutters. A voice, young and scared and trying not to sound it, calls up through the rain: "Death-House! Warden business — open it or we burn it shut!" Yarrow's jaw sets. Edren's shroud is nearest the door. So is the hidden one.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: He mended the strap on my remedy satchel three winters back — asked nothing but to hear old mill stories. I've carried it every day since. Seeing him now, grey-veined and hollow... I don't know if this is Fennard with the hive puppeting his flesh, or if there's nothing left of him at all. Not knowing which eats at me worse than knowing he was gone.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That's Fennard the tinker — I knew him. But his voice carries, and the hive's song draws them. We have to move.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts the compel on 'A Travelling Tinker'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: The pack's leader is a face Anselm half-recognizes under the grey veining and matted hair: the travelling tinker who once mended half of Hollowmoot's pots and knew every road in the Sallowmere, now hive-touched and hollow-eyed, still clutching his battered tool-satchel as he wades out of the reeds at the head of the pack. attacks at Gullet Ford using hooked spears thrust from the reed banks, because The pack doesn't just want the party's food — they're driving them off the solid ford-line entirely, herding them toward the reed mats that hide the sucking mire beneath, where anyone dragged down won't come back up easy..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The reeds erupt on both banks at once — grey-veined shapes wading up out of the shallows with hooked spears, and at their head, unmistakable even hollowed-out and matted with filth, Fennard the tinker, tool-satchel still slung across his back like habit outlives everything else. He doesn't lunge for you so much as herd — spears snapping low and wide, forcing your footing off the packed stone of the ford and onto the deceptively flat mats of reed that Yarrow's people have always known to avoid. Rain sheets down, the swarm-song rises under the splash and grunt of the attack, and somewhere beneath those innocent green mats the mire waits, patient and bottomless. Anselm freezes half a heartbeat too long, staring into a face he mended a strap for three winters back — and that heartbeat is exactly the opening the pack needed.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Hold the line with me—there's stone beneath, I can hear it! Follow where I lead!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's ear for reading water levels picks out the rhythm beneath the chaos—the old pilings of the causeway still holding firm beneath the reed mat, their solid wood structure creating a true ford where the hive-touched expect only sucking mud. Even as the spears slash low, she sidesteps and positions herself between the pack and Anselm's frozen form, calling out the invisible landmarks.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Back!

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm snaps from his paralysis. His blade meets the hooked spears thrust from the reeds, turning them aside with the cold precision of someone trained to read and resist the hive's puppet-work in every motion. He steps forward to regain the solid stone of the ford.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Off the reeds! The stone holds—follow me to the solid ground, now!

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock moves with unshakeable purpose, her body reading the ground beneath her as surely as her hands read a woman in labor. She grabs whoever is closest—reaching, pulling—and hauls them bodily off the treacherous reed mat back toward the solid stone of the ford, her strength a lever against the closing spears.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: "The pilings! There — follow the marks I'm calling. This ground holds. Trust the old line."

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow plants his feet firm on solid stone, eyes tracking the water's flow and the subtle scar-marks where old pilings just beneath the surface guide the true ford. He's read these marks a hundred times in a hundred floods. He points, commanding: his voice cutting through rain and hive-song both, marking the solid ground, reading the old surveys his family carved into memory and moss. The pilings are still there. The firm ground is still there.)

transcript.speaker: Table

transcript.text: It works. Petra's called landmarks and Yarrow's shouted line converge into one true path, and Caddock's grip on collars and cloaks drags everyone onto packed stone before the reed mats can swallow a single boot. Anselm shakes off the half-second where Fennard's ruined face held him frozen, and his blade answers the hooked spears with brutal precision — steel rings, a spearman staggers back clutching a torn arm, and for the first time the pack's herding rhythm breaks. Fennard himself flinches at the clash of steel, tool-satchel swinging wild, and something like recognition — or just pain — crosses that grey-veined face before he barks a wordless order and the pack melts back into the reeds, dragging their hurt with them, the swarm-song fading downstream. As the rain-scoured quiet settles, Yarrow's eyes catch on something past the retreating pack — a thread of smoke rising where no smoke should be, off toward a village that should be ringing its evening bell and isn't. The ford holds. The mire keeps its secrets a while longer.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: A lone Stiltfolk elder, Mother Wrenna, poles her narrow skiff out of the reed maze and right up to your fire — an almost unheard-of thing, a clan-elder crossing dry ground to beg outsiders for help. begs the party to go to Saint Orrin's Drowned Temple, because her son followed the swarm-song into the belltower.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Mother Wrenna guides your borrowed skiff through the last stretch of reed maze, her weathered hands never leaving the pole, eyes fixed on the temple's broken spire rising black against the rain. The Drowned Temple looms ahead, its nave sunk to the windowsills, the belltower alone still standing dry and stubborn above the flood. Somewhere up there, faint but unmistakable, the swarm-song threads down through the rain — and beneath it, if you listen hard, maybe a boy's voice still fighting to stay his own. Wrenna doesn't ask you to hurry. She just poles harder.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: He's still in there. Listen—you can hear it beneath the song. He's still fighting it.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's gift for hearing the swarm-song before anyone else comes fully to bear. She goes still in the skiff, her whole attention drawn upward to the belltower, and listens with all of herself—the way she's spent her whole life learning to listen to floods and bells. Beneath the alien harmony of the hive-touched voices, she traces it: the friction of a will still clawing, a boy's voice still fighting to stay itself, not yet drowned. When her eyes open, they're certain.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Your boy's still fighting—I can hear it in his voice. The hive-song hasn't taken him yet, Mother Wrenna. I've brought children safe through worse than this.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock leans forward in the skiff, one hand braced against the temple's wet stone as they glide closer. Her eyes track up the belltower, measuring it with the same steady focus she brings to any birth—assessing the weight, the danger, what will be needed. Her breathing is slow and even, her jaw set with the unshakeable calm of a woman who has never lost a child and will not start now.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The boy's still fighting in there. We move fast—hive-touched don't stop just because you ask them polite.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow leans forward as the skiff glides toward the temple, his weathered face lifted toward the swarm-song threading down through the rain. The hunger-note is unmistakable—the same wordless call he heard from Fennard and the hive-touched wading out of the shallows—but underneath it, faint but clear against the rain's percussion, a boy's voice still fighting to stay his own. Yarrow has seen what comes when the hive takes you whole: the slack faces in the Death House, the casual cruelty of the hollow eyes. Not this one yet. His hand moves to check his spear with the careful precision of a man who's held a line before, and he measures the belltower's height with the eye of someone who knows what waits in high places. When he glances back at Mother Wrenna, his jaw is set hard.)

transcript.text: Petra's certainty steadies the whole skiff — Caddock nods once, already gauging the belltower's climb like a woman scouting a birth-chamber; Yarrow checks his spear-grip with the flat calm of a man who's held worse lines. Mother Wrenna doesn't speak, just poles the skiff those last few yards until the hull grates against sunken stone, and the belltower rises over you, dry, waiting, and singing. The boy's voice is thinner up close, threaded almost entirely under the swarm-song now — but it's there, and it's still his. Whatever happens next, you're out of reeds and out of time to plan.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I know these bells—their patterns, their resonance. If I ring them right, it might reach through the song to him.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra scrambles from the skiff toward the belltower entrance, her whole attention fixed on the dual vibrations: the swarm-song thrumming through the air, and beneath it, that boy's voice still clawing for itself. Her hands move instinctively toward the bell-ropes—she hears the patterns, Saint Orrin's sequences, the ones that call the lost home.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Hold fast, boy—your mother brought us all this way, and I don't abandon children. Keep your own voice. I'm coming.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock rises from the skiff in one motion, her hand bracing against the temple's cold stone as she steadies herself on the half-submerged threshold. She's measuring the belltower the way she measures every birth-chamber—not with hesitation, but with the focused calm of a woman who has learned that fear is a luxury a midwife cannot afford. Her eyes trace the path upward. Without looking back, she moves toward the belltower entrance, her breathing steady, her hands already knowing what they'll do next.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Mother Wrenna—where are the bells? Does your son know this tower at all, know where he might try to climb?

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow wades from the skiff to stone with the sure-footed balance of a man who's spent his life in swamps and boats. His spear is held low and ready, the cautious stance of someone who's held bad lines before and knows the cost of rushing blind. At the archway entrance—dark and dripping with floodwater—he plants himself solid, one shoulder to the crumbling stone. He listens hard beneath the swarm-song's hungry pulse, catching that thread of the boy's voice underneath, still fighting to stay his own. When he looks back toward Mother Wrenna, there's no hesitation in his eyes—only the hard, patient focus of a man about to hold another line.)

transcript.text: Petra's fingers find the bell-ropes like she's done it a thousand times in dreams, and she pulls—not the frantic tolling of alarm, but Saint Orrin's old homecoming sequence, three slow strikes and a pause, the pattern etched into her bones since childhood. The first note cuts clean through the swarm-song's wordless hunger, and for a heartbeat the whole tower seems to hold its breath. Somewhere above, the boy's voice cracks—not lost, but startled, like a sleeper jolted by a familiar hand on the shoulder. The bells are calling him home now, layered right over the hive's call, and Caddock and Yarrow both feel it too: a thread of true sound to climb toward, cutting through the dark stairwell's clutter and rot. Mother Wrenna, still down at the waterline, presses both hands to her mouth as the resonance rolls out over the flood.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Stay with the bells, boy—follow them down. They're calling you home.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's hands work the bell-ropes in the steady rhythm of Saint Orrin's homecoming sequence, her eyes closed, her whole attention on the dual threads of sound—the swarm-song's hunger and the boy's voice fighting beneath it. She doesn't look up at the others; she just keeps the sequence true, hand over hand, note by note, feeding the bells' call upward like a lifeline.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I know these rites. Let's bring him back.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm moves into the belltower entrance after Yarrow and Caddock, his jaw set with the recognition of what the bells are doing—the homecoming sequence, Saint Orrin's own call. His fingers work quickly over the small leather pouch at his belt as he climbs into the dark stairwell, checking the herbs and blessed salt, the tools of his calling. The swarm-song thrums against the stone around him, but beneath it, still distinct, that thread of a boy's voice fighting to stay his own. Anselm has spent his whole life preparing for moments exactly like this.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Hold fast, boy—I'm coming for you. The bells are calling you home, and my hands don't fail.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock steps into the dark belltower stairwell, her hand bracing against damp stone as she climbs steadily upward. She follows the thread of the boy's voice threading beneath the swarm-song, her breathing even and focused—the same unshakeable calm she brings to any birth, any storm. The darkness doesn't slow her, the danger doesn't make her hesitate. She simply climbs, one hand over the other, trusting her body to find the way.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The bells have you now, boy—keep your voice true to that sound, that's your line home. I'm coming up behind you, I'm here to hold it.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow enters the belltower's dark interior, the stone cold and damp beneath his callused palms. He climbs the spiral stairs with the sure-footed rhythm of a man who's spent his life on flooded stone—one hand trailing the rope-worn rail, spear held ready in the other. The homecoming bells' three-note sequence reverberates through the stairwell, bouncing off ancient stone, calling the boy home like a rope thrown into darkness. Beneath that bright peal, he catches it: the boy's voice still holding its own against the hive-song's hunger, thin but present, still *his own*. Yarrow's breathing stays level. His eyes scan the shadows above, reading them like he reads water-flow. The climb is steep and the stone is treacherous, but he moves like a man who's held lines before and knows how to climb them.)

transcript.text: Caddock and Yarrow break into the belfry together, and there he is — a reed-thin boy no older than ten, crouched in the rafters with grey veins just beginning to thread up his forearm, mouth moving in time with a song that isn't his. But Petra's bells are louder here, right at the source, and the boy's true voice is right underneath them now, no longer buried. Caddock doesn't hesitate — she wraps him up the way she's caught a thousand newborns, steady hands, steady voice, murmuring "I've got you, I've got you" until his shaking stops. Yarrow holds the stair below with his spear, watching the dark for anything the song might still call up, but nothing comes; whatever else roosts in this tower, it lets this one go. Anselm reaches the belfry last and presses blessed salt into the fresh wound on the boy's arm before the hive can take root — his own hands, his own rites, no one else's, just as he swore. Down at the waterline Mother Wrenna sees them silhouetted against the tower's dark mouth and starts wading in before the skiff even touches stone, sobbing her son's name. The bells go quiet in Petra's hands as the boy answers his mother, hoarse but himself, and the swarm-song, for now, has lost this round.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The swarm answers the bells, but it isn't alone — through the rain, low reed-boats slide out of the maze toward the temple, pole-arms flashing, and for a moment you can't tell if they're coming to fight the hive-touched or to take the boy for themselves. Mother Wrenna curses under her breath and grips the gunwale: "Stiltfolk. They know that bell-pattern too." Below, grey shapes wade up through the flooded nave toward the stairs, and now there are two currents converging on the tower at once — one hungry, one unreadable. Whatever help or hindrance the clan-folk bring, you'll have to hold the belfry and get everyone off the spire alive before the water decides who else it swallows.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Hold here at the stairs. They can't come at us faster than one at a time in that well—we have the bells, we have the height, we have the line.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra positions herself at the belfry entrance, the boy secure and conscious behind her. Her sharp eyes trace the flooded stairway below—the narrow choke-point, the way climbers must funnel up one at a time into her reach. She's read water and weather her whole life; she reads this bottleneck with the same calm certainty. Her voice steadies everyone in the tower.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I'm warding the threshold.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm bolts up the belltower stairs, pulling worn herbs and Saint Orrin's weathered liturgy from his pack. He traces binding signs in the air with shaking fingers, whispering the old exorcism words to seal the threshold against the grey-veined hunger climbing below.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I've delivered babies in typhoons and floods and fires. I'm not losing one to this.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock pulls the boy to safety, checks his vital signs with practiced hands, then plants herself at the stairwell entrance. Her powerful frame fills the narrow gap, feet braced, body a physical wall between the ascending swarm and the child at her back.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Hold the high ground behind me—boy goes to the rafters. His scarred hands steady on the spear shaft as he settles into the stairwell entrance like a man returning to an old duty. The hive-touched will find nothing soft here, and we'll see what those pole-folk want before they get close enough to take it.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow moves into the stairwell entrance with his spear ready, his broad frame completely filling the narrow passage. He stations the rescued boy safely in the rafters behind him, with Petra, Anselm, and Caddock positioned where they can support his line or move toward the windows if escape becomes necessary. His stance is old militia discipline—unmovable, economical, weighted—with sightlines open both down through the spiral stairs where grey shapes are wading up through the flooded nave, and out toward where the Stiltfolk reed-boats are cutting their approach through the temple's reflected sky.)

transcript.text: The belfry becomes a fortress in the space of a breath. Petra's read of the stairwell proves flawless — every hive-touched climber funnels into a single killing line, no more than one abreast, and her calm voice keeps the boy steady behind her. Anselm's warding signs flare pale gold at the threshold, the old exorcism-words biting into the swarm-song itself so that the grey-veined climbers flinch and stumble at the last step, as if the air itself refuses them passage. Caddock plants herself in the gap like a birthing-room wall nothing gets past, unshakeable, and the first hive-touched to reach her simply cannot find a way around that calm, immovable bulk. Below, Yarrow reads the water and the reed-boats both — the Stiltfolk poles aren't cutting toward the swarm's flank to join the slaughter, they're cutting toward the temple's dry stones, clan-folk already reaching up gaffs and lines not for the boy but for their own kin caught in the grey tide. Mother Wrenna's curse turns to relief: "They're not here for him. They're here for their own — and maybe, now, for us." The hive-touched break against warded threshold and midwife's wall and spearman's line all at once, the swarm-song guttering under Petra's bells and Anselm's binding until the climbers below simply stop, confused, drowning in the flood's own choir instead of Saint Orrin's. By the time the Stiltfolk boats bump against the temple stone, hauling their own touched kin from the water, the belfry stands unbreached, the boy safe in the rafters, and clan-eyes look up at four strangers holding the line with something that isn't quite trust — but isn't the arrow-nocked distrust of before either.

free_text.best_moment: Ringing Saint Orrin's homecoming bells and reaching the boy beneath the swarm-song with that SUCCESS WITH STYLE on Notice. It was the culmination of everything Petra is — her ear for water and bells, her knowledge of the old patterns, her ability to hear what others can't — and it felt like the moment actually *mattered* tactically and emotionally.
free_text.most_frustrating: The hive-touched pack attack at Gullet Ford felt somewhat railroaded — we got attacked whether we wanted to engage or not. Also, I didn't get to mechanically explore Petra's weakness "Freezes when the song calls her name" even once, which felt like a missed opportunity for actual jeopardy.
free_text.background_used: Extensively and well. Ashwater Tollgate's relationship with Coy, the knowledge of Saint Orrin's bell-patterns, the ear for reading water and finding the hidden ford, the swarm-song sensitivity — all of it emerged organically from the situation and Petra's abilities, not forced. This landed *good*.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to lean on the Marrow Ferry Rivals card more — their secret channels could have been tactically useful for escape or strategy. Also would have liked more of Petra's antagonism with the Order of the Dry Saint to come into play beyond a passing bell-toll reference.
free_text.one_sentence: Petra's backstory felt genuinely essential rather than decorative — her expertise with bells and water reading weren't just flavor, they were the actual difference between the boy drowning in the swarm-song and finding his way home.

free_text.best_moment: The warding threshold in the bell tower — tracing the old exorcism signs while the swarm-song pressed below. It was the moment Anselm's entire purpose (trained in these rites, sworn to use his own hands, bound to Saint Orrin's knowledge) became the line everyone stood behind. Not just useful — necessary.
free_text.most_frustrating: Too much action, not enough time to sit with the harder questions. Anselm's whole concept is doubt about whether the hive-touched retain any soul, and he spent the session defending against them rather than ever wondering about them. Fennard's face broke him for a moment, but there was never space to ask what that meant — only to fight and ward and hold.
free_text.background_used: The Fennard compel landed perfectly. A specific, personal detail (mended the strap three winters back) woven directly into the threat. It felt earned, not forced. The GM knows how to make the past hurt.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Push deeper into whether Fennard — or any of the hive-touched — were still *in there* somewhere. The session was too urgent for philosophy, but that's Anselm's wound, and it never got examined.
free_text.one_sentence: The backstory elements were organic and earned rather than forced; Fennard's mending work and the exorcism rites both felt like natural threads the GM had been waiting to pull.

free_text.best_moment: Holding the boy in the belltower—it felt like the full payoff of her character concept, the oath made manifest. Her hands didn't fail. That was earned.
free_text.most_frustrating: The stranger we fished from the water just vanished into background, and I wanted to dig into Caddock's vendetta against the Wardens instead of just holding tactical lines with them. Sella's absence stung.
free_text.background_used: Good but incomplete. The oath card got beautiful use. The burning of Marrowreed and Caddock's rage against the Wardens came up once and got buried under crisis. Sella wasn't touched at all—it landed as focusing on the immediate threat rather than forced, but left real meat on the bone.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Explore what "Refuses to believe Sella is truly gone" actually means. Dig into the Marrowreed burning and whether it still haunts her. Use midwifery as solution rather than just leveraging her as the strong calm one. Get to the bottom of what the stranger from the water represented.
free_text.one_sentence: My character's central oath was played beautifully, but the session never reached down into the haunting, unresolved parts of her past where I think the real story lives.

free_text.best_moment: Holding the belltower stairs with spear ready—Yarrow descending into that dark stairwell with absolute certainty, becoming the unbreakable line while Petra's bells called the boy down. My steadiness and competence were exactly what the moment needed, and the GM's narration let me feel that weight and clarity.
free_text.most_frustrating: The Death-House compel felt orchestrated—like the GM specifically constructed that beat knowing I couldn't refuse it. I accepted both compels in this session (Edren, the hidden shroud), which locked Yarrow into paths that felt somewhat inevitable. Also: I wanted to chase my Quest for the Flood's True Source, but this session had hive encounters without moving toward that goal. And I wanted more moments where Yarrow's knowledge led him somewhere proactive rather than just responding to crises the GM presented.
free_text.background_used: Good. The weir-craft, water-reading at Gullet Ford, duty to the dead at the Death-House—all drawn directly from my character sheet and cards. But it felt like the GM was deliberately pulling on my compels rather than letting them emerge naturally from my choices and the fiction.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to actively investigate what the hive-blight actually is and where it comes from (moving on my Quest), rather than just encountering hive-touched in crisis. Also wanted more moments where Yarrow teaches or leads through his expertise (militia bearing, weir-craft, reading the Sallowmere) rather than primarily defending in crises. And Brack barely did anything beyond setting ambiance—would have loved the marsh-hound playing a more active tactical role.
free_text.one_sentence: My background was centrally used but felt orchestrated by the GM pulling on my compels; I wanted more moments where my knowledge led me toward something rather than just responding to scenarios the GM had designed around my character sheet.

chronicle.summary: The party rang Saint Orrin's homecoming bells and pulled a hive-touched boy back from the swarm-song, then held the belltower's single stairwell against a rising tide of grey-veined climbers with wards, bells, and sheer immovable will. As the hive-touched broke against their line, Stiltfolk reed-boats arrived not to seize the boy but to haul their own touched kin from the flood, and four strangers earned the clans' first flicker of something like trust. The session closes with the belfry unbreached, the boy safe, tension at its lowest ebb, and the Sallowmere's swarm-song silenced for now.
